8000:
To hunch means to bend or curve your upper body — especially your back and shoulders — forward or inward, so that your body forms a rounded, folded shape. It is a physical action involving your posture.

Picture someone sitting at a desk, leaning forward with their back rounded and their shoulders pulled upward and inward toward their chest. That person is hunching. The body is no longer upright and straight — it is curved, like the letter C.
What Exactly Moves When You Hunch?

The action focuses on two areas: your back and your shoulders.

When you hunch, your shoulders rise up and move forward, and your upper back rounds and curves outward. Your head often tilts slightly downward as a result. The body makes itself smaller and more closed-in. It is the opposite of standing tall with your chest open and shoulders back.

Understanding why people hunch helps you understand the word deeply. People hunch for several reasons:

1. To protect themselves from the cold or wind.
When it is freezing outside, a person naturally pulls their shoulders up toward their ears and curves their body forward, as if trying to trap warmth inside. This is instinctive.

She hunched against the icy wind as she walked to the bus stop.

2. When concentrating deeply on something.
When someone is very focused — reading a book, writing, working on a computer, or looking at a phone — they often lean forward and round their back without even noticing it.

He hunched over his notebook, scribbling notes quickly.

3. Out of fear, anxiety, or trying to look smaller.
When people feel afraid, nervous, or want to avoid attention, they sometimes physically make themselves smaller by hunching. It is a defensive posture.

The boy hunched in the corner, not wanting to be noticed.

4. Out of habit or tiredness.
Some people simply hunch because they are tired or have poor posture habits, especially when sitting for long periods.

After eight hours at the computer, she was hunching badly.
How the Word Is Used Grammatically

"Hunch" as a verb works in two ways:

A. With an object (transitive) — you hunch a specific body part.
Here, you are describing what part of the body is being curved. The most common phrase is "hunch your shoulders."

He hunched his shoulders and said nothing.
She hunched her back to fit under the low ceiling.

B. Without an object (intransitive) — the whole body hunches.
Here, no specific body part is named. The verb describes the overall posture.

He hunched over the map, trying to find the right road.
Don't hunch — sit up straight.

The most frequently used form of this verb is "hunch over" something. It means to bend your body forward over something, getting close to it with your back curved.

She hunched over her phone for so long that her neck started to hurt.
The old man hunched over the chessboard, thinking carefully.
"Hunched" — The Adjective Form You Will See Often

Once you hunch, you are in a hunched position. "Hunched" is used as an adjective to describe a person whose posture is curved and bent forward. You will see this form very commonly.

He sat hunched at his desk all evening.
A hunched figure walked slowly through the rain.
She looked tired and hunched.

Think of "hunched" as the state of being — you are in the position that hunching creates.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words all describe bent or lowered body positions, but they are not the same:

Hunch — the upper body (back and shoulders) curves forward. The legs may or may not be involved.

Crouch — you bend at the knees and lower your whole body close to the ground, like a sprinter at the starting line, or someone hiding behind a wall.

Stoop — you bend the upper body downward from the waist, usually to reach something below you, like picking something off the floor.

Slouch — you sit or stand in a lazy, sloppy way with your body drooping. It carries a sense of carelessness or laziness, while hunching is more about actively curling inward.

The clearest difference: hunching is about rounding and curling the upper body inward, particularly the back and shoulders. It is tighter and more self-contained than the others.

To hunch is to curve your upper body — your back arching outward and your shoulders drawing up and forward — into a rounded, closed posture. It happens when people are cold, focused, afraid, or simply tired. It is the opposite of standing straight and open. The word is most often used with "over" (hunch over something) or with a body part (hunch your shoulders), and its adjective form "hunched" is equally common in everyday writing and speech.
8001:
Hunched describes a body posture where the upper back is rounded and curved outward (like an arch), the shoulders are pulled inward or raised upward, and the head leans forward. Instead of standing or sitting tall and straight, a hunched person bends their upper body into a curved, compact shape — making them look smaller, tighter, and folded into themselves.

Think of the letter C. A hunched back looks roughly like that curve.
What It Looks Like — A Clear Picture

Imagine a person sitting at a computer for hours. Over time, without realising it:

  • Their upper back starts to round and curve outward
  • Their shoulders roll forward and inward
  • Their neck pushes their head forward
  • Their chest caves in slightly
  • They look smaller than they actually are

That is a hunched posture. The body is no longer open and upright — it is folded, curved, and closed in.

"Hunched" is not just one thing. People become hunched for many different reasons, and the word covers all of them:

Physical causes:

  • Cold — When you are freezing, your body naturally pulls the shoulders up and in to protect itself and stay warm. "She walked through the icy wind, hunched against the cold."
  • Pain or injury — Someone with a sore back or stomach might curl inward to protect the painful area.
  • Old age — Over many years, the spine can gradually curve forward, making a person permanently hunched. This is very common in elderly people.
  • Illness or weakness — A sick or very tired person may lack the strength to hold themselves upright.

Emotional and mental causes:

  • Sadness or depression — A sad or defeated person often physically collapses inward. The body reflects the mood.
  • Fear or nervousness — When people feel small, scared, or threatened, they unconsciously make themselves physically smaller by hunching.
  • Shyness or low confidence — People who are self-conscious often hunch to take up less space, as if trying to disappear.

Situational causes:

  • Deep concentration — "He sat hunched over his notebook, writing furiously." When someone is intensely focused on something in front of them — a book, a screen, a piece of work — they lean into it and curve their body forward.
  • Habit — Many people simply develop a hunched posture over years of sitting badly, looking at phones, or working at desks.

You will very frequently see "hunched over" followed by an object. This means the person is bending their curved upper body over something specific:

  • "She was hunched over her phone."
  • "The old man was hunched over his walking stick."
  • "The students sat hunched over their exam papers."

"Hunched over" always implies both the curved posture AND a direction — the body is leaning toward something.

A person's full posture:
"The hunched figure stood alone in the rain."
(The entire body looks bent and curved.)

Shoulders specifically:
"He walked in with hunched shoulders."
(Just the shoulders are raised and pulled inward — the most common physical sign of being cold, scared, or sad.)

A figure or silhouette:
"In the dim light, I could see a hunched shape sitting in the corner."
(The shape itself tells you the person is curved and bent.)

Animals too:
A cat that is frightened or cold will arch its back and pull itself inward — that is also described as hunched.

These words are close in meaning but not identical:

Hunched vs. Slouched:
Slouched is relaxed and lazy — your body just loosely sags because you are not bothering to sit up. There is no tension. Hunched is more compressed and tighter — the shoulders pull in, the back curves with more intention (even if unconscious). You can slouch on a sofa carelessly. You hunch in the cold or over a desk.

Hunched vs. Stooped:
Stooped usually describes a more permanent, ongoing condition — especially in older people whose spine has curved with age. Stooped is what you are. Hunched is often what you do in a moment or situation, though it can also be permanent.

Hunched vs. Crouched:
Crouched is about bending the knees and lowering the whole body downward — like a sprinter at the starting line, or someone hiding. The legs do the work. Hunched is specifically about the upper back and shoulders curving inward and forward. The legs are not the point.

Because of all the situations in which people hunch — cold, sadness, fear, exhaustion, age — the word carries a strong emotional weight. When a writer says someone is hunched, they are rarely just describing a posture. They are signalling something about that person's inner state or situation:

  • A hunched figure in a story often feels small, tired, defeated, burdened, or vulnerable.
  • A character who straightens up from a hunched position is often recovering strength, courage, or dignity.

The opposite of hunched — standing tall, shoulders back, spine straight — communicates confidence, power, and openness. Hunched is the physical opposite of that.

• "The cold was so fierce that every person on the street walked hunched, trying to stay warm."
  • "Years of working at a desk had left him permanently hunched."
  • "She sat hunched in the corner of the waiting room, staring at the floor." (suggests sadness or anxiety)
  • "The boy came home hunched and quiet — something had clearly gone wrong at school." (emotional defeat)
  • "The old woman moved slowly, her hunched back making her look half the height she once was."
  • "He was so hunched over the tiny screen that his neck would surely ache later."

Hunched means having the upper back curved and rounded outward, with the shoulders drawn inward or upward and the head pushed forward — a posture that makes a person look bent, smaller, and closed in, caused by cold, age, tiredness, sadness, fear, or deep focus.
8002:
A hunger strike is a deliberate, voluntary refusal to eat food — and sometimes drink water — as a form of protest or pressure. A person who goes on a hunger strike is not starving because they have no food. They have food, but they choose not to eat it. That choice is the whole point.

It is a way of saying: "I want something so badly — or I object to something so strongly — that I am willing to harm my own body, or even risk my life, to make my point."

For something to truly be called a hunger strike, three things must be present:

  1. It is intentional. The person makes a conscious, deliberate decision to stop eating.
  2. It is public or known. The refusal to eat is announced to someone — an authority, the public, or the media. A private fast is not a hunger strike.
  3. It is tied to a demand or a cause. The person wants something specific to happen, or wants to draw attention to an injustice. Without a goal, it is not a strike — it is just not eating.

A hunger strike is a weapon of the weak against the powerful. It is used when a person feels they have no other way to be heard.

Think about it: if someone is in prison, they cannot march in the streets. If a group has no political power, they cannot pass laws. But they do have control over their own bodies. By threatening serious harm to themselves, they force others — governments, institutions, or the public — to pay attention.

The logic is essentially: "Look at what your actions are forcing me to do to myself." It puts moral pressure on those in power. It says: if I suffer or die, that is on your conscience.

The power of a hunger strike comes from two places:

  • The body as leverage. As days pass without food, the body weakens visibly. Weight drops. Organs begin to fail. This creates a ticking clock that the public and authorities cannot easily ignore.
  • Moral force. The striker is not hurting anyone else. They are only hurting themselves. This makes it very difficult for opponents to dismiss or attack them without looking cruel. It generates sympathy.

People go on hunger strikes for many different reasons. Common demands include:

  • Release from prison or detention
  • Recognition of political rights or human rights
  • Better treatment of prisoners
  • Protest against an unjust law or policy
  • Drawing international attention to a cause that is being ignored

The human body can survive without food for roughly 30 to 70 days, depending on the person's size, health, and whether they are drinking water. Within the first week, a person feels intense hunger but is not in danger. After two to three weeks, the body begins breaking down muscle and fat for energy. After several weeks, organ damage begins. Death is the final outcome if the strike is not ended.

A hunger striker who drinks water survives longer than one who refuses both food and water. Refusing water (a dry hunger strike) is far more dangerous and can lead to death within days.

It ends in one of three ways:

  1. The demand is met — the authority gives in, fully or partially, and the striker agrees to eat.
  2. The striker gives up — they decide to end the strike without winning their demand, either because their health is failing or because they change strategy.
  3. The striker dies — the most extreme outcome, which can turn them into a martyr and sometimes causes the very change they were seeking, even after death.

In some cases, authorities respond by force-feeding the striker — inserting a tube into their nose or throat to pour nutrients into their body. This is deeply controversial. Many medical and human rights organizations consider force-feeding a form of torture and a violation of a person's right to make decisions about their own body.

It is important not to confuse a hunger strike with:

  • Fasting for religious or health reasons — a personal choice with no political dimension.
  • Starvation due to poverty or famine — involuntary and not a form of protest.
  • A diet or detox — voluntary but not tied to any demand or cause.

The word "strike" is key. Just like a labor strike (where workers refuse to work to demand better conditions), a hunger strike is a strategic refusal — not a passive suffering, but an active, purposeful act.

The word "strike" here carries the same meaning as in phrases like "workers' strike." It means a deliberate stoppage of something as an act of resistance. Just as workers stop their labor, a hunger striker stops consuming food — both as a form of controlled, intentional protest aimed at forcing change.

A hunger strike is when a person publicly refuses to eat — and sometimes drink — in order to protest an injustice or pressure someone in authority to meet their demands. It is a nonviolent but potentially fatal act of resistance. Its power comes from the moral weight of self-harm: it forces the world to watch, feel responsible, and respond.
8003:
To hunker means to squat down low — to bend your knees deeply and drop your body close to the ground, almost like sitting on your heels without actually sitting. Your body becomes small and low. Imagine a baseball catcher crouching behind home plate, a child bending down to get a closer look at an ant on the sidewalk, or a soldier ducking behind a wall. That physical position — low, crouched, compact — is hunkering.

It is almost always followed by the word "down", making the phrase "hunker down."

While the physical meaning is real, the far more common and powerful use of "hunker down" is figurative — meaning it describes a mindset and behavior, not just a body position.

To hunker down figuratively means to settle in, hold your ground, and endure a difficult or demanding situation — usually for a long period. You are not running away. You are not quitting. You are planting yourself firmly and preparing to get through it, whatever it is.

Think of it this way: just like crouching physically makes you harder to knock over, hunkering down mentally means you are making yourself stable, determined, and resistant to whatever is coming at you.
What "Hunker Down" Feels Like in Real Life

Here are the situations where people naturally use "hunker down":

  • A storm is coming. Families board up their windows, stock up on food, and stay inside. They hunker down and wait for the hurricane to pass. They are not fighting the storm — they are enduring it by staying put and staying prepared.
  • You have a huge exam in two days. You cancel your plans, sit at your desk, and study for hours and hours without distraction. You hunker down and get it done.
  • A business is going through a financial crisis. The company stops spending money on new things, cuts costs, and focuses on surviving. They hunker down until the hard times pass.
  • A soldier or athlete is in a tough situation and refuses to give up. They dig in, stay focused, and push through. They hunker down.

In every case, notice these shared ideas:

  • Something difficult is happening or about to happen
  • The person chooses to stay and face it (not escape)
  • There is effort, patience, and determination involved
  • It often involves a period of waiting or enduring, not just acting
The Emotional Tone of the Word

"Hunker down" carries a strong feeling of toughness, resilience, and no-nonsense determination. It is not a panicked or desperate word. It is a grounded word. When someone says they are hunkering down, they sound calm, practical, and ready. It almost has a soldier-like or survivor-like toughness to it.

It can also sometimes carry a slightly negative shade of meaning — suggesting someone is being stubborn, refusing to change, or retreating into a defensive position rather than adapting. For example: "The politician just hunkered down and refused to answer any questions." Here, hunkering down means being closed off and uncooperative. Context always tells you which shade is meant.

• The hikers hunkered down in their tent as the snowstorm grew worse.
  • She hunkered down and finished the entire project in one weekend.
  • After the market crashed, the investors hunkered down and waited for recovery.
  • The children hunkered down behind the sofa during the thunderstorm.
  • Instead of adjusting their strategy, the team just hunkered down and repeated the same mistakes.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

DimensionWhat it means

Physically: To crouch low to the ground, making your body small and stable.

Figuratively (most common): To commit yourself fully to enduring or pushing through a hard situation — staying put, staying focused, and not giving up, usually over a sustained period of time.

Feeling of the word: Tough, grounded, determined, practical — and occasionally, stubbornly defensive.

If you remember one image for this word, make it this: a person crouching low in a storm, holding steady, not moving, not breaking. That is hunkering down — both literally and in spirit.
8004:
Imagine a soldier in a trench ducking low to avoid gunfire. Or a child pulling a blanket over their head during a thunderstorm. Or a student switching off their phone, sitting at their desk, and refusing to move until the exam paper is finished.

All three of these people are doing the same thing in spirit — they are hunkering down.

"Hunker down" means to settle yourself firmly into a position and stay there, either to survive something difficult or to focus intensely on something important. It carries the feeling of lowering your head, bracing yourself, and holding steady against whatever is coming.

Before it became a common expression, "hunker down" had a very physical meaning. To hunker means to crouch low or squat on your haunches — your haunches being the area of your upper thighs and buttocks. Think of how a baseball catcher squats low behind the batter. That position — low, stable, compact, close to the ground — is "hunkering."

So at its most literal, "hunker down" just means to physically get low and stay low. It is a stable, grounded crouch, not a careless collapse.

This physical image is the heart of the whole expression. Everything else the phrase means comes from this core picture: getting low, making yourself small and stable, and staying put.

The word "hunker" is old. It likely comes from Scottish and Northern English dialects, possibly related to Dutch and Low German words meaning "to squat" or "to crouch." In older Scottish English, people would say someone was "on their hunkers," meaning they were crouching down on their heels.

The phrase traveled into mainstream English over the centuries and eventually became common in American English, where it picked up its broader figurative meanings.
The Three Main Meanings in Modern Use

Today, "hunker down" is used in three closely related but slightly different ways.

Meaning 1: To prepare for and survive something difficult

This is the most common use. When bad things are coming — a storm, a crisis, a tough period — you do not run. You get into a safe, protected position and you wait it out.

Think of a family nailing boards over their windows before a hurricane. They are not going anywhere. They are settling in, staying put, and bracing for what is coming. That is hunkering down.

Examples:

  • "The whole city hunkered down as the blizzard arrived."
  • "During the economic recession, the company hunkered down and cut all unnecessary expenses."
  • "We hunkered down in the basement when the tornado warning was issued."

The key feeling here is: stay where you are, protect yourself, and endure. It is not about escaping. It is about surviving in place.

Meaning 2: To focus deeply and work hard on something

Sometimes you have a big task — a difficult assignment, an important project, an exam to prepare for. You close all distractions, sit down, and give it everything you have. That is also hunkering down.

Here, the "staying put" is about your attention and effort, not a physical storm. You are settling into serious work and refusing to be distracted.

Examples:

  • "I have three essays due on Friday, so I'm going to hunker down this weekend."
  • "The team hunkered down for the final month before the product launch."
  • "She hunkered down in the library every evening until she passed her exams."

The feeling here is: put your head down, stop wasting time, and get the work done.

Meaning 3: To stubbornly hold your position and refuse to change

This meaning is used most often in politics or arguments. When someone is being criticized or pressured to change their mind — and they refuse — they are "hunkering down."

Here, the image is of someone planting their feet, crouching low, and refusing to be moved no matter what force is applied against them. It can be seen as strength or as stubbornness, depending on the context.

Examples:

  • "Despite public backlash, the politician hunkered down and refused to resign."
  • "The company hunkered down on its controversial policy despite customer complaints."
  • "He hunkered down and wouldn't admit he was wrong, no matter how much evidence he was shown."

The feeling here is: dig in, resist pressure, and do not give an inch.

Even though these three uses look different on the surface, they all share the same emotional core:

  1. You are facing something difficult or demanding.
  2. You are not running away.
  3. You are lowering yourself into a firm, stable position.
  4. You are staying put and seeing it through.

The phrase always carries a sense of determination and endurance. There is something slightly tough and gritty about it. It is never casual. Hunkering down means you are serious.
The Tone and Feeling of the Phrase

"Hunker down" has a sturdy, no-nonsense, practical feeling to it. It does not sound dramatic or heroic. It sounds like the thing a sensible, hardworking person does when conditions are tough. It is the language of survival and focus, not panic.

Compare it to a phrase like "brace for impact" — that sounds alarming and sudden. "Hunker down" sounds calm and deliberate. It is what you do when you know something hard is coming and you have decided to handle it steadily.
Common Situations Where You Will Hear It

• Weather and natural disasters: Storms, hurricanes, snowstorms, floods — this is where the phrase feels most natural.
  • Work and studying: Deadlines, exams, big projects — when focus and effort are needed.
  • Business and finance: Companies cutting costs, surviving downturns, or pushing through difficult periods.
  • Politics: Leaders or parties refusing to change course when pressured.
  • Personal challenges: Any hard stretch of life — illness, loss, difficulty — where someone is just getting through it quietly and steadily.

The phrase can be used with "for" (to prepare for something specific) or on its own:

  • "We need to hunker down for the winter months." — preparing for a specific difficult period
  • "It's time to hunker down." — just get focused and serious, no specific event needed
  • "The country is hunkering down as the crisis deepens." — describing an ongoing state

You will mostly see it in American English, though it is understood widely across the English-speaking world.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you want one image to carry with you:

"Hunker down" is what you do when a storm is coming and you cannot run — you crouch low, hold tight, and you wait it out.

From that single image, every other use of the phrase makes sense. Whether the "storm" is bad weather, a difficult project, or outside pressure trying to change your mind, the response is always the same: get low, hold steady, and don't move.
8005:
"Hunt down" is a phrasal verb. It means to search for someone or something persistently, thoroughly, and with great determination — and to eventually find them.

The key idea is not just searching, but searching until you succeed. You don't give up. You keep going until you track your target down.

Think of it like a predator chasing its prey in the wild. The predator doesn't search casually — it follows every clue, every trail, every footprint until it finds what it's looking for. That intense, unstoppable energy is at the heart of "hunt down."

Understanding the two parts of the phrase separately helps you understand why they work together so powerfully.

"Hunt" means to search for something or someone, or to chase and pursue prey. It already suggests effort and purpose — you're not stumbling upon something accidentally; you're actively going after it.

"Down" is the part that adds the feeling of completion and thoroughness. In English, "down" is often used in phrasal verbs to suggest that something has been fully achieved or brought to a conclusion — like "track down," "pin down," or "nail down." When you add "down" to "hunt," it signals that the search doesn't stop halfway — it ends in success.

So together: hunt + down = pursue relentlessly until found.
What Makes This Phrase Special (The Nuance)

This is the part many learners miss, and it's what separates a good understanding from a great one.

"Hunt down" carries several strong implied meanings beyond just "find":

1. The target is hard to find.
You don't "hunt down" your pen when it rolls under your desk. The phrase is used when the target is hidden, missing, elusive, on the run, or very difficult to locate. There is genuine difficulty in the search.

2. The searcher is determined and relentless.
There is no passive waiting. The person doing the hunting is actively pursuing, following leads, overcoming obstacles, and refusing to stop.

3. The target usually doesn't want to be found.
When used about a person, "hunt down" almost always implies that the target is hiding, fleeing, or evading. A criminal running from the police. A wanted person in hiding. This gives the phrase a tense, sometimes threatening energy.

4. The outcome is eventual success.
This is very important. "Hunt down" strongly implies that the search ends with the target being found. It's not just the act of searching — it's the act of searching and succeeding. If someone says "The police hunted down the suspect," you understand that the suspect was eventually caught.

"Hunt down" has a serious, intense, and often forceful tone. It is not gentle or casual language.

When used about a person, it can feel threatening or aggressive — because it implies someone is being pursued like prey. It is commonly used in news reports, crime stories, legal contexts, action narratives, and thriller novels.

However, the phrase can also be used in a lighter, more casual way when talking about objects, information, or hard-to-find things — though even then, it keeps its sense of determination and difficulty.

Seeing a phrase in many different contexts is one of the best ways to truly own it. Here are examples that cover the full range of how "hunt down" is used:

1. Hunting a Person (Most Classic Use)

"The detective spent three years trying to hunt down the killer."

Here, a criminal is hiding and evading capture. The detective is relentless and determined. The search is long and difficult. This is the most typical and powerful use of the phrase.

"Authorities finally hunted down the fugitive after he fled to another country."

A fugitive is someone who has escaped and is hiding. "Hunted down" tells you that despite the evasion, they were eventually found and caught.

"He feared that his enemies would hunt him down wherever he went."

Notice here — "hunt him down" — when the object is a pronoun (him, her, them, me, you, it), it must go in the middle of the phrasal verb, between "hunt" and "down." This is a grammar rule for this type of phrasal verb. More on this below.

2. Hunting an Animal (The Literal, Original Sense)

"The villagers hunted down the wolf that had been attacking their livestock."

This is close to the original, literal meaning — a physical chase of an animal that ends in capture or killing. The wolf was causing harm and hiding, and the villagers pursued it until they found it.

3. Hunting for Information, Objects, or Things (Figurative Use)

This is where the phrase becomes more flexible and less threatening:

"She spent months hunting down rare first-edition books for her collection."

The books aren't running away, of course — but they are difficult to find. "Hunting down" conveys the effort, persistence, and determination involved in finding something very hard to locate.

"I finally hunted down the source of the strange noise in my car."

Again, lighter use — but the sense of determined, persistent searching is still there. Finding the source wasn't easy; it took effort.

"The journalist hunted down every piece of evidence before publishing the story."

Here it's used about gathering information — suggesting thorough, relentless research.
Grammar: How to Use "Hunt Down" Correctly

"Hunt down" is a transitive phrasal verb, which means it always needs an object (the thing or person being hunted). You cannot say "They hunted down" without completing the sentence.

Here are the key grammar rules:

Rule 1: With a noun, you can place it after "down" OR between the two words.

Both of these are correct:

  • "The police hunted down the suspect."
  • "The police hunted the suspect down."

Rule 2: With a pronoun (him, her, it, them, me, you), it MUST go in the middle.

This is correct:

  • "The police hunted him down."

This is incorrect:

  • "The police hunted down him."

This rule applies to most separable phrasal verbs in English, and "hunt down" follows it strictly.

Rule 3: It can be used in all tenses.

  • Present: "They are hunting down the suspect."
  • Past: "They hunted down the suspect."
  • Future: "They will hunt down anyone responsible."
  • Perfect: "They have hunted down every lead."
Similar Phrases That Are Worth Knowing

Understanding "hunt down" becomes even richer when you compare it to related expressions:

Track down — Very similar to "hunt down." It means to find someone or something after a long search. However, "track down" is slightly less intense and doesn't carry as strong a sense of danger or aggression. You might "track down" a phone number or an old friend, but you'd "hunt down" a criminal.

Run to ground / run down — To chase someone until they have nowhere left to escape. Very similar energy to "hunt down." Common in British English.

Chase down — To catch up to someone who is running or moving away. More about the physical chase, less about the detective-style persistent search.

Root out — To find and remove something harmful that is hidden, such as corruption or a traitor. Similar determination, but with more emphasis on exposing something hidden within a group or system.

Ferret out — To uncover something hidden through clever, patient searching. Used more for information or secrets than for people on the run.
A Quick Way to Remember It

If you want one clear image to remember this phrase forever, picture this:

A bloodhound — a hunting dog — following a scent trail through forests, over rivers, across fields. It doesn't stop. It doesn't get distracted. It keeps following that trail no matter how long it takes or how difficult the terrain is, until it finds what it's looking for.

That bloodhound is "hunting something down."

TypePhrasal verb (transitive, separable)
Core MeaningTo search with great persistence and determination until you find someone or something
Key NuanceThe target is hard to find, often hiding or evading; the seeker is relentless; the search ends in success
ToneIntense and serious; lighter when used figuratively about objects or information
Grammar NotePronouns must go in the middle: "hunted him down," not "hunted down him"

"Hunt down" is a powerful, vivid phrase that paints a picture of a relentless, determined pursuit that does not end until the target is found. Once you truly feel the energy behind it — that unstoppable, bloodhound-like determination — you'll recognize it instantly and use it with confidence.
8006: The word "hurdle" carries two concrete, real-world meanings and one abstract meaning that you will encounter constantly in everyday language. All three are important, and understanding how they connect will make the word feel natural to you.
Meaning 1: A physical barrier in an athletic race

A hurdle is a lightweight, upright frame — shaped like a small rectangular bar held up on two legs — that is placed on a running track for athletes to jump over as they sprint. In track and field competitions, a series of these frames are lined up at equal distances along a straight lane, and athletes must leap over each one without stopping. The sporting event is itself called "the hurdles."

She knocked over the fourth hurdle but still finished the race in second place.

One important physical detail: athletic hurdles are designed to tip forward if a runner's leg hits them. They are not rigid walls. They are meant to fall, which reduces the risk of injury. This detail matters because it directly gives birth to the figurative meaning of the word — more on that below.

When you hear "hurdles" as the name of a sport (e.g., "She competes in the 100-metre hurdles"), it refers to the entire race or athletic discipline.
Meaning 2: A movable fence panel (traditional/agricultural use)

In an older and more traditional sense — still used in rural and farming contexts, particularly in British English — a hurdle is a portable rectangular frame or panel, typically made of wood or woven branches, used to build a temporary fence. Farmers would set up rows of these movable panels to pen in sheep or other livestock, then dismantle and move them to a different spot as needed.

The shepherd arranged the hurdles into a small pen to separate the lambs from the rest of the flock.

You are less likely to hear this meaning in modern everyday conversation, but you may come across it in older literature, farming discussions, or rural settings. It is worth knowing so the word never catches you off guard.
Meaning 3: An obstacle, difficulty, or challenge (figurative — the most important meaning)

This is the meaning you will encounter most frequently in daily life, news, conversations, and writing. A hurdle, in this sense, is any problem, difficulty, or obstacle that stands between a person and a goal they are trying to reach. It is something that must be dealt with or overcome in order to move forward.

Getting government approval was the biggest hurdle the company faced before launching the product.
She cleared every legal hurdle and finally received her licence.
Raising enough funds remains the final hurdle for the project.

The key feeling that the word "hurdle" gives is this: the obstacle is real and demanding, but it is not impossible to overcome. Calling something a hurdle implies it is a challenge to be cleared, not a dead end. This is an important nuance. If someone says "that's a major hurdle for us," they mean it is a serious difficulty they need to tackle — not that they have given up. The word carries a sense of effort and determination within it.
How the three meanings are connected

The figurative meaning (Meaning 3) flows naturally and beautifully from the athletic meaning (Meaning 1). Think about a hurdle race: a runner must leap over one barrier, then the next, then the next, in order to keep moving toward the finish line. If they stop, they lose. If they jump cleanly and keep going, they win.

Life, work, and ambition work the same way. There are obstacles placed between you and what you want, and you must deal with each one — clear it, get over it, move on — to keep making progress. That is exactly why we borrowed the image of a physical hurdle and turned it into a word for life's difficulties.

Also notice that athletic hurdles are designed to fall if hit — they are not immovable walls. This reinforces the figurative sense perfectly: a hurdle in life is something that can be overcome with the right effort.
Common words and phrases used with "hurdle"

Certain verbs and phrases are very naturally paired with "hurdle" in its figurative sense. These are the combinations you will hear most often:

Clear a hurdle — to successfully get past an obstacle.
The startup cleared its first major hurdle by securing funding.

Face a hurdle — to encounter an obstacle.
Every new business faces countless hurdles in its early stages.

Overcome a hurdle — to successfully deal with a difficulty.
He overcame every hurdle on his path to becoming a doctor.

The final hurdle / the last hurdle — the last obstacle remaining before achieving something.
Passing the bar exam is the final hurdle before she becomes a lawyer.

A major hurdle / a significant hurdle — a big or important obstacle.
Language was a major hurdle for immigrants trying to find work.

Jump over / get over a hurdle — same meaning as "clear a hurdle."
Once we get over this regulatory hurdle, we can begin construction.

To put it all together simply: a hurdle is either a physical frame that athletes jump over in a race, a movable wooden fence panel used on farms, or — most commonly — any challenge or obstacle in life that you must overcome to reach a goal. The word always carries the idea that the obstacle is real but passable. It asks for effort, not surrender.
8007:
To hurl something means to throw it with great, forceful energy. Not a gentle toss, not a casual throw — but a throw that involves your whole body, your full strength, and often a burst of intense emotion. When you hurl something, there is real power and urgency behind it.

Think of it this way: if you lightly toss your keys to a friend, you "throw" them. But if you're furious and you fling a plate across the room with all your might, you hurl it. The difference is force and intensity.

Here are some clear examples:

  • The pitcher hurled the ball toward the batter at full speed.
  • The protestors hurled rocks at the windows.
  • She picked up the book and hurled it across the room in anger.

In all these cases, something is launched through the air with serious force. The thing being thrown doesn't have to be heavy — what matters is the intensity of the action.
The Key Quality That Sets "Hurl" Apart

The single most important thing to understand about "hurl" is that it almost always carries a sense of violence, force, or strong emotion. This is what separates it from ordinary words like "throw," "toss," "fling," or "pitch."

Think of these comparisons:

  • "He threw a stone into the lake." → casual, ordinary action.
  • "He hurled a stone at the car." → aggressive, forceful, emotionally charged.

When a writer or speaker chooses the word "hurl," they are deliberately signaling that something intense is happening — physically or emotionally.

"Hurl" is very commonly used in a non-physical, figurative way — especially when talking about words, accusations, insults, or abuse. When someone attacks another person with harsh, angry language, we say they hurl those words.

  • The politician hurled accusations at his opponent.
  • The angry customer hurled insults at the staff.
  • Protesters hurled abuse at the officials as they walked by.

Why does this work? Because just like physically hurling an object, hurling words is an aggressive, forceful act aimed directly at someone. The words are "launched" at a target with the intent to hurt or damage. The imagery is powerful and accurate.

In informal, everyday speech — especially in American English — "hurl" is also a slang term meaning to vomit. This usage is casual and slightly humorous in tone.

  • The ride was so intense that he almost hurled.
  • She ate too much and ended up hurling.

This meaning is informal. You wouldn't use it in formal writing or professional settings, but it's widely understood in casual conversation.
When to Use "Hurl" vs. Similar Words

Since "hurl," "throw," "toss," "fling," and "pitch" all involve sending something through the air, it helps to know when "hurl" is the right choice.

Use "hurl" when you want to emphasize raw force, violence, or strong emotion. If the action feels explosive, desperate, or angry, "hurl" fits perfectly. If the action is routine or calm — like passing something to a colleague — a simpler word like "throw" or "toss" is more natural.
To hurl is to throw something with great and forceful intensity — and by extension, to aggressively direct harsh words at someone, or informally, to vomit.
8008:
When you use hurly-burly as an adjective, you are describing something that is full of noisy, wild confusion and frantic, turbulent activity. It paints a picture of a situation, place, or way of life where everything seems to be happening at once — loudly, chaotically, and at a breathless pace. Nothing is calm or orderly. Everything is in motion, in noise, and in a kind of excited disorder.

Think of a busy fish market at its peak hour. People are shouting prices, vendors are rushing around, buyers are haggling, fish are being thrown across stalls, water is splashing, and the whole place is one giant blur of noise and movement. That is a hurly-burly scene.
Breaking Down What It Actually Describes

A hurly-burly thing has three qualities working together, all at the same time:

1. Noise. It is never quiet. There is shouting, clattering, arguing, laughing, or the general roar of many things happening at once. Silence has no place in anything hurly-burly.

2. Disorder and chaos. There is no neat structure or clear order. Things overlap, interrupt each other, and happen in no particular sequence. It can feel like controlled (or uncontrolled) madness.

3. Frantic energy and constant movement. People and things are always rushing, always active, never still. The pace is relentless. There is no pause, no breath, no moment of peace.

When all three of these come together — the noise, the chaos, and the frantic energy — you have something that deserves to be called hurly-burly.
Examples That Bring It to Life

• "He grew tired of the hurly-burly world of politics."

Here, the speaker is saying that the world of politics is exhaustingly chaotic — full of shouting, arguments, constant activity, and disorder. It never settles down, and it wears people out.

  • "She stepped away from the hurly-burly life of the city to find peace in the countryside."

The city life being described is noisy, fast, overwhelming, and disordered. It's the opposite of calm and quiet.

  • "The hurly-burly atmosphere of the stock exchange made him nervous."

The stock exchange floor — with traders yelling, phones ringing, numbers flashing, and everyone rushing — fits this perfectly.

  • "Children at play create a wonderfully hurly-burly scene."

Here the word is used warmly. The chaos is joyful — kids running everywhere, screaming, laughing, bumping into things — a happy, noisy mess.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is important: hurly-burly is not always negative. It depends entirely on the context.

Sometimes it carries a sense of exhaustion or criticism — as if to say, "This is all too much. It's overwhelming and I want out." (Like the politics example above.)

Other times it carries a sense of excitement or nostalgia — as if to say, "Yes, it's chaotic and loud, but it's also alive and thrilling." (Like a bustling street market or a lively childhood memory.)

The word itself does not judge. It simply describes the quality of turbulent, noisy, chaotic energy — and you, the speaker, decide whether that's wonderful or exhausting through your tone and context.

It's important to know what hurly-burly does not imply:

  • It does not mean violent or dangerous. A war zone is not typically called hurly-burly. The word feels too playful and lively for something truly threatening.
  • It does not mean quietly messy. If something is disorganized but silent, it is not hurly-burly. The noise is essential.
  • It does not mean evil or morally wrong. It carries no moral judgment — it is purely about the energy and character of a scene or way of life.

Hurly-burly is not an everyday word you will hear in casual conversation. It has a slightly literary, old-fashioned, and colorful feel to it. You are more likely to find it in writing, in journalism, in books, or used by someone who enjoys expressive language. When a writer or speaker chooses this word, they are making a deliberate choice — they want you to feel the noise and chaos, not just understand it. The word itself sounds chaotic, which is part of its charm.

Hurly-burly (adjective) describes something that is noisily chaotic, frantically busy, and turbulently disordered — a world or scene where everything is loud, fast, and happening all at once, with no stillness in sight.
8009:
Imagine a football match. The striker kicks the ball and it flies into the net. Instantly, thousands of fans jump to their feet, pump their fists in the air, and scream in joy. That loud, joyful cry — that burst of collective excitement — that is a hurrah.

A hurrah is a shout or cry of joy, triumph, approval, or enthusiasm. It is the sound that comes out of people when something wonderful or exciting happens.

Meaning 1: A Shout or Cry of Excitement

This is the most direct meaning. A hurrah is a vocal expression of joy, celebration, victory, or approval — a cheer. It can come from one person or from a whole crowd.

Think of it this way: when something great happens, people don't just feel happy silently. They express it loudly. That expression — that outburst — is a hurrah.

Examples:

  • The soldiers let out a hurrah when they heard the war was over.
  • A hurrah went through the crowd as the winner was announced.
  • She finished her speech and was greeted with hurrahs from the audience.

Notice that in these sentences, a hurrah is a real, physical thing you can hear — it is a sound, a cry, something produced by people in a moment of strong positive emotion.

It can also be used in the plural — hurrahs — when there are many such cheers happening, or when the cheering goes on repeatedly.

  • The stadium filled with hurrahs after the final goal.

Meaning 2: A General State of Excitement, Fuss, or Commotion

Less commonly, "hurrah" can refer to a noisy, exciting situation — a general buzz or commotion surrounding something. Here, it moves slightly away from a single shout and becomes more of a mood or atmosphere of excitement.

  • There was quite a hurrah around the opening of the new store.

This usage is less frequent in modern English, but it is worth knowing.

In modern English, the most widely used form of this noun is in the phrase "last hurrah." This is so common that you will encounter it constantly — in newspapers, books, conversations, and sports commentary.

A last hurrah means:

A final effort, act, achievement, or celebration before something ends — especially the end of a career, a life, or an era.

It carries a sense of finality mixed with grandeur. It is the idea that something or someone is doing something significant one last time before the curtain falls. It is often bittersweet — exciting and celebratory, but also tinged with the sadness of an ending.

Examples:

  • The aging champion fought brilliantly in what many called his last hurrah.
    (He is near the end of his career, and this fight was his final great moment.)
  • The band reunited for a world tour — a last hurrah before officially disbanding.
    (They came together one final time to celebrate what they built before splitting up permanently.)
  • The retiring CEO launched one ambitious new product as her last hurrah.
    (Before she left her job, she did one final impressive thing.)
  • The summer festival felt like a last hurrah before the cold months arrived.
    (It was the final joyful event before a long, dull period.)

The key feeling behind "last hurrah" is this: it is glorious, but it is goodbye.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Hurrah" is not a neutral word. It always carries energy and emotion. When you see it used as a noun, you should feel:

  • Excitement — something good is happening or has happened
  • Collective spirit — often, it involves groups of people sharing a feeling
  • A peak moment — a hurrah marks a high point, not an ordinary moment

In the case of "last hurrah," add to that a layer of nostalgia and farewell — the joy is real, but so is the awareness that it won't happen again.

• A hurrah is always positive in tone — you would never call a sad or angry outcry a hurrah. It is specifically tied to joy, approval, or triumph.
  • It implies spontaneity — hurrahs are not planned, polished speeches. They are raw, instinctive outbursts of feeling.
  • When used in the plural (hurrahs), it suggests either multiple cheers or sustained, repeated cheering.
  • "Last hurrah" is often used in journalism and commentary to describe the final impressive act of a career or era, and it works even when there is no literal shouting involved — it is purely figurative.
A hurrah is a joyful shout or cheer of excitement and triumph; and a last hurrah is a final glorious effort or moment before something or someone comes to an end.
